..
Issued at 343 AM CDT Thu Sep 17 2026

Currently, surface high pressure is situated over southern
Saskatchewan and Manitiba, and into northeast North Dakota.
Clear to partly cloudy skies were noted across western and
central ND, but patchy fog was indicated on Satellite and looks
to be increasing in areal coverage. The extent of fog and
possible hazards will be the main forecast issue in the short
term period. 

After today, the focus shifts to an impulse that tracks across
South Dakota tonight into Friday morning, bringing 
precipitation to far southern ND, then to western ND this
weekend as an upper level low approaches the area. 

The impulse tonight should bring some beneficial light rains to
far southern portions of the forecast area. Yesterday at this 
time there was a northward trend in the qpf. If anything, today 
the trend is back south, with only the far southern tier 
counties seeing more than a tenth of an inch. The probability 
for at least a quarter inch of rain from 1 AM Friday to 1 AM 
Saturday, is around 50 percent over the far southern James River
Valley, and quickly tapers as you go north.

There is another area of showers, and possibly a thunderstorm 
that models continue to focus on, the northwest portion of the 
state, and possibly into the far north central. An area of 
elevated instability is situated from northeast MT/northwest ND 
and into southern Manitoba, ahead of an approaching northern 
stream wave and associated cold front. This is also within an 
area of strong warm advection and increasing moisture transport 
ahead of the Canadian cold front. Unless you get a thunderstorm,
don't think the qpf amounts will amount to much up here, with 
the higher totals remaining in southern Canada. The latest NBM 
is showing low to medium probabilities (20 to 60%) for at least 
a quarter inch over northwest ND in the 24 hour period ending 7 
PM Friday. That instability axis lingers through Saturday along 
the International Border, but qpf amounts here remain light with
high pressure situated over southern Manitoba.

The upper level low will be tracking through the Northern 
Rockies and into the Northern High Plains Saturday through 
Saturday night, then into the Northern Plains Sunday through 
Sunday night. Overall, the trend has been drier with this 
system. The track of the upper level low looks to be farther 
south. We see sort of a High over Low blocking pattern develop 
with an upper level ridge and surface high pressure situated 
over southern Canada, keeping the track of the low to our south 
and limiting the northward extent of moisture. QPF totals 
continue to diminish over western ND. QPF totals in western ND 
from Friday evening through Sunday evening range from a quarter 
to a half inch, and are mostly limited to the far northwest and 
far southwest, with less than a couple tenths most areas. On
Monday, the upper low exits the area and any low precipitation
chances will be limited to southern portions of the forecast
area. Beyond Monday, there may be another wave bringing some 
low precipitation chances mid-week, but uncertainty in this 
remains high. 

Temperature wise we remain seasonable with high temperatures
remaining mainly in the 60s and 70s and low temperatures in the
40s to lower 50s. There is a signal for a gradual warming trend
as we head through the work week, with deterministic and 
ensemble models showing an upper level ridge over the central 
portion of the U.S. by the end of the work week. However there 
is uncertainty as to whether or not this is a strong ridge 
yielding warmer temperatures, or a flatter ridge in our neck of
the woods, keeping temperatures closer to normal. Although NBM 
ensemble temperatures do increase gradually through the week, 
NBM ensemble temperature spreads also increase through the week.
Confidence in a gradual warming trend in medium to high, but 
confidence in a significant warm-up, although possible, remains 
low at this time.
